facts.claim: UNESCO page title is 'Three genres of traditional dance in Bali' (Indonesia), inscribed in 2015 (10.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. UNESCO describes three genres: sacred, semi-sacred, and dance meant for enjoyment by communities at large, accompanied by gamelan.

UNESCO's description does NOT mention weddings or name the genres wali, bebali or balih-balihan; it says the dances 'symbolize particular traditions, customs and religious values' and tags the element with 'Rituals' and 'Ritual purification'. So the article may say UNESCO recognises three genres, one meant for enjoyment by communities at large, but must not say UNESCO links them to weddings.

Australian Embassy Indonesia 'Marriage in Indonesia' page: DFAT and its missions cannot advise on other countries' specific marriage requirements; contact the nearest Indonesian Embassy/Consulate-General or the Indonesian Civil Registry Office (Catatan Sipil) where the marriage will take place. The page is 'a general guide only'.

Embassy page: generally persons of any nationality may marry in Indonesia provided they hold a religion recognised by the Indonesian Government (page lists Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism or Christian); marriages may be performed by ministers of religion, Civil Registry Office officers or the Office of Religious Affairs (KUA); for a marriage to be legal it must be conducted according to the religion and conform to the laws of the countries of the parties.
Embassy page, heading 'Couples must be of the same religion': under Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974 concerning marriage, both parties must hold the same religion; if not, one party must convert.

Embassy page: an Australian citizen marrying in Indonesia needs a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) from the Australian Embassy Jakarta or the Consulates-General in Denpasar (Bali), Surabaya or Makassar. The Consulate-General Bali covers Bali, NTB and NTT. CNI usually issued while you wait if documents are complete; no expiry is set, but local Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept CNIs issued more than 3 months prior. You cannot marry at the Embassy/Consulate-General. No fee is stated on this page.

Embassy page: Muslim weddings are performed by the Office of Religious Affairs (KUA), which issues the Marriage Book (Buku Nikah); civil registration is usually not required but a Civil Registry marriage certificate is recommended if relocating. Non-Muslim marriages (Christian, Hindu, etc.): lodge a Notice of Intention to Marry with the Civil Registry Office at least 10 days before the wedding, and after the ceremony the marriage must be registered at the Civil Registry Office to be legal. Documents: CNI, passports, birth certificates, proof of dissolution of a previous marriage or death certificate (if applicable), four 4x6 cm photos; requirements vary by province.

Embassy FAQ: since 1 January 1995 a marriage legally performed overseas that would have been legal in Australia is accepted as legal under Australian law; you do not register it with the Embassy and cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia.

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (updated 18/08/2026): you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is recognised if valid where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred here; Australia doesn't recognise overseas marriages where a party is already married, underage, too closely related or forced. DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country; ask the destination's embassy whether it needs authentication or apostille. Talk to a lawyer to confirm validity.

Smartraveller Indonesia (updated 21 October 2026): overall 'Exercise a high degree of caution' (level 2); 'Reconsider your need to travel' (level 3) for Papua Pegunungan and Papua Tengah; Bali is not in a higher-level area. Aceh applies Sharia law, which bans same-sex relationships and cohabitation before marriage among other things. Missions: Embassy Jakarta; Consulates-General Bali, Makassar, Surabaya.

Undergraduate thesis abstract (Lailan Nadiyah, UIN Antasari, 2020, studying Bugis-Makassar people in Bontang, East Kalimantan): uang panai is different from the Islamic mahar; it is given by the groom's side to the bride's family, is used to pay for the wedding celebration and is meant to show respect to the bride's family; in adat it is treated as an obligation and a precondition of the wedding, while the agreed amount depends on agreement between the two families and factors such as social standing, descent, education and economy. Academic (student thesis) source, one community; no amounts used.

Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974 on Marriage is listed as in force ('Berlaku') on the BPK legal database (JDIH BPK), enacted 2 January 1974, amended by Law No. 16 of 2019; the Constitutional Court decision 22/PUU-XV/2017 concerned the minimum marriage age in Article 7(1). The article text itself (e.g. Article 2 on validity by religion and registration) was not read in this pass; rely on the Australian Embassy summary (fact_103, fact_104).

Pawiwahan is the Hindu wedding ceremony; the word comes from 'wiwaha', from Sanskrit, meaning wedding celebration. The study defines it as a sacred ceremony in which a man and woman bind themselves as husband and wife, through a purification carried out both physically and spiritually (sekala and niskala); it counts as a Manusa Yadnya rite. It involves three 'witnesses': Bhuta saksi (the mabyakala rite), Dewa saksi (offerings and announcing at the family shrine, sanggah/pamerajan) and Manusa saksi (customary village officials, family and guests).
facts.source: https://jurnal.stkipahsingaraja.ac.id/index.php/wspah/article/download/74/50 (Ningsih & Suwendra, 'Upacara Pawiwahan dalam Agama Hindu', Jurnal Widya Sastra Pendidikan Agama Hindu 3(2), 2020; literature-based study)

facts.claim: The study lists the pawiwahan sequence as: choosing an auspicious day by the Balinese Hindu calendar; ngekeb (preparing the bride); the groom's family collecting the bride; mungkah lawang (knocking at the bride's door, with Balinese songs); mesegeh agung (welcome at the groom's home); mekala-kalaan or mabyakala; mewidhi widana; and mejauman (also called mepamit).
facts.source: https://jurnal.stkipahsingaraja.ac.id/index.php/wspah/article/download/74/50 (Ningsih & Suwendra, 'Upacara Pawiwahan dalam Agama Hindu', Jurnal Widya Sastra Pendidikan Agama Hindu 3(2), 2020; literature-based study)

facts.claim: Mekala-kalaan / mabyakala, per the study: a purification of the couple led by the ceremony leader after a puja; bamboo (tetimpug) is burned until it cracks; the couple step over it three times, face the pabyakalaan offerings, have their hands cleansed, touch a raw egg with their toes, are sprinkled with holy water (melukat), walk around the offerings, and finally break a white thread (benang pepegatan) to mark entering married life (grahasta).
facts.source: https://jurnal.stkipahsingaraja.ac.id/index.php/wspah/article/download/74/50 (Ningsih & Suwendra, 'Upacara Pawiwahan dalam Agama Hindu', Jurnal Widya Sastra Pendidikan Agama Hindu 3(2), 2020; literature-based study)

facts.claim: Mewidhi widana is led by a high priest (sulinggih / Ida Pedanda), followed by prayers at the groom's family shrine led by the family-temple priest (pemangku), to tell the ancestors a new member has joined; mejauman/mepamit takes place at the bride's family shrine, where she takes leave of her own ancestors as she becomes part of the groom's family. In the common Balinese form (memadik) the bride joins the groom's family; in nyentana the man joins the woman's family.
facts.source: https://jurnal.stkipahsingaraja.ac.id/index.php/wspah/article/download/74/50 (Ningsih & Suwendra, 'Upacara Pawiwahan dalam Agama Hindu', Jurnal Widya Sastra Pendidikan Agama Hindu 3(2), 2020; literature-based study)

facts.claim: Suntiang is a gold-coloured, multi-tiered headdress worn by Minangkabau women; it is one of the most important elements of traditional wedding dress and is worn by the anak daro (bride). It forms a half-circle of flora and fauna ornaments (e.g. roses, bananas, peacocks, butterflies, fish). Original suntiang were made of gold, silver and copper; many are now lighter coated aluminium. The study gives a weight of about 3.5 to 5 kg and says the weight symbolises the responsibility a Minang woman carries after marriage, with newer pieces smaller and lighter. ABSTRACT ONLY, read via Garuda (Kemdiktisaintek index): Mustika & Budiwirman, 'Analisis Fungsi dan Makna Suntiang dalam Pakaian Adat Minangkabau', Gorga: Jurnal Seni Rupa 8(2), 2019, DOI 10.24114/gr.v8i2.14712.

Suntiang gadang is described as the bride's headdress in Minangkabau, particularly in Padang Pariaman, with plant and animal motifs that carry moral messages for the couple (Yulimarni & Yuliarni, Ekspresi Seni 16(2), 2014, ISI Padang Panjang, DOI 10.26887/ekse.v16i2.82). Styles and names vary by area (e.g. suntiang mangkuto in Tanah Datar). ABSTRACT ONLY via Garuda.

Ulos is the Batak woven cloth; literally 'blanket'. Giving ulos is called mangulosi and symbolises love from giver to recipient; in Batak customary weddings there is a mangulosi stage for the bride and groom, and informants said a Batak couple is considered officially married (in adat) after it (Kristina & Yusuf, JOM FISIP Universitas Riau 6(2), 2019). Ulos is also used at births and deaths. ABSTRACT ONLY via Garuda.

Toba Batak customary marriage sequence per a University of North Sumatra law journal abstract (Hutauruk, Jurnal Civil Law USU 1(1), 2019): visit to the woman's family, giving a token (tanda holong), marhusip, marhata sinamot, pudun saut, martumpol, pamasu-masuon (blessing), then marhata adat followed by mangulosi. Mangulosi follows kinship position; ulos types named include ulos pansamot, ulos hela, ulos pamarai, ulos todoan and ulos sihunti ampang. A separate abstract (Tama & Lephen, Acintya 15(2), 2023, ISI Surakarta, DOI 10.33153/acy.v15i2.5117) places mangulosi within the ulaon unjuk ceremony. ABSTRACTS ONLY via Garuda.

Mangulosi is giving the woven cloth from someone of higher standing to another as a sign of blessing, placed on the recipient's shoulders; ulos is used at customary weddings, house-warmings, births, baptisms, for honoured guests and at times of mourning (Butar-Butar et al., Jurnal Pendidikan Tambusai 8(2), 2024). ABSTRACT ONLY via Garuda.

insider_details.detail: For a legal (not symbolic) wedding in Bali, the Embassy guidance means planning backwards from the Civil Registry: the Notice of Intention to Marry goes in at least 10 days before the ceremony, and a CNI older than about 3 months is not normally accepted, so get the CNI from the Consulate-General in Bali inside that window. As at November 2026; check with the embassy and the registry, including any fees.

The Embassy summary of the Marriage Law says both partners must hold the same recognised religion or one must convert, which is why many Australian couples marry legally at home and hold a blessing or celebration in Bali; an overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia but is generally recognised if valid where it took place.

A Balinese Hindu wedding is a sacred family rite at home and at the family shrine, led by priests (a pemangku at the family temple, a sulinggih or pedanda for mewidhi widana); treat the purification (mekala-kalaan) as something the families and their priest decide on, not a styled resort add-on.

UNESCO recognises three genres of Balinese dance (sacred, semi-sacred and dance for enjoyment by communities at large) but says nothing about weddings, so the safe advice is to ask a local cultural adviser which dances are appropriate to perform for guests rather than booking a sacred dance as entertainment.

A traditional suntiang is heavy (one study gives roughly 3.5 to 5 kg, with lighter modern versions), so a Minangkabau bride wearing one for a long reception needs fittings, rest breaks and a dresser on the day; plan the photo schedule around it.
At a Toba Batak adat wedding, mangulosi follows kinship order and can take a long time, so build generous time into the run sheet and let the families' spokespeople lead it.
